queries.diagnose: Resolve fades when the mind runs ahead to the feeling or looks sideways at the prize; it holds when the work itself is the reward.
queries.steady: No honest effort on the right path is ever wasted; even a little of it protects you and carries you forward.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse.sanskrit: श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात् । स्वभावनियतं कर्म कुर्वन्नाप्नोति किल्बिषम् ॥
verse.line: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.
verse.translation: Better is one's own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed. Doing the work born of one's own nature, one incurs no wrong.
verse.why: Do the work that fits you, flaws and all, as an offering.
verse.misuse: Not 'stick to the role you were born into'. It's about honest fit with your own nature, not caste or family script.

prasang.title: Duties by nature, and their fruit
prasang.summary: After listing duties by varna, Krishna says one reaches perfection through one's own work done as worship, and that one's own path, though imperfect, beats another's, since every undertaking has flaws.
prasang.lesson: Do the work that fits you, flaws and all, as an offering.

verse.meaning: Arjuna is on the battlefield, paralyzed by what he must do. Krishna tells him that his own duty, even if it is messy or hard, is better than doing someone else's job perfectly. Doing the work that matches your own nature brings no fault upon you, because it is an offering. The point is to stop comparing your path to another's and to walk your own, flaws and all.
verse.for_you: You quit your job because the work felt like yours. That is your own path, imperfect and alive. When the first hard month arrives, you will not need borrowed energy. You will only need to trust the work that matches your own nature. Your own work is your own offering.
verse.try_today: Notice one task today that feels like it belongs only to you.
verse.scene_line: You are on the edge of a choice, and the work is yours.
asks: How do I tell when the work is truly mine?
What if my own path is not enough?
How do I stay on my own path?

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: From the section praising learning: the three kinds of people.
verse.sanskrit: प्रारभ्यते न खलु विघ्नभयेन नीचैः प्रारभ्य विघ्नविहता विरमन्ति मध्याः ॥ विघ्नैः पुनः पुनरपि प्रतिहन्यमानाः प्रारब्धमुत्तमगुणा न परित्यजन्ति ॥
verse.line: Some never start for fear of obstacles; some quit when obstacles hit. The best keep going.
verse.translation: The lowest do not begin at all, for fear of obstacles. The middling begin, but stop when obstacles strike. The best, struck by obstacles again and again, do not give up what they have begun.
verse.why: What you learn and how you speak are the wealth no one can take from you.
verse.misuse: Perseverance is not refusing ever to change course; weigh honestly whether the goal still deserves you.

matched.label: I can't tell if continuing is discipline or stubbornness

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: In praise of learning and the learned
prasang.summary: Bhartrihari praises learning as wealth no thief can take and speech as the one lasting ornament, then turns to good company and the three kinds of people who face obstacles. It ends with the 'sword's-edge vow' of the good.
prasang.lesson: What you learn and how you speak are the wealth no one can take from you.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to the reader about learning, describing three kinds of people. The lowest never begin, afraid of obstacles. The middling begin, but stop when obstacles strike. The best are struck again and again, and they do not give up what they have begun. This means the path you are building is yours to walk, and the resolve to keep going is the real wealth no one can steal.
verse.for_you: The alive feeling you have now is real, but it will fade. The test is not the first day, but the long month when only the work remains. Keep going anyway, because the resolve is the wealth. Your own path is the one to walk.
verse.try_today: Notice when the alive feeling fades and the work feels like work.
verse.scene_line: You are the one who keeps going when the path gets hard.
asks: How do I know when to push through and when to change?
How do I keep going when no one is watching?

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.sanskrit: निन्दन्तु नीतिनिपुणा यदि वा स्तुवन्तु लक्ष्मीः समाविशतु गच्छतु वा यथेष्टम् । अद्यैव वा मरणमस्तु युगान्तरे वा न्याय्यात्पथः प्रविचलन्ति पदं न धीराः ॥
verse.line: Let them praise or blame, let money come or go: the steady don't step off the right path.
verse.translation: Let the worldly-wise blame or praise; let fortune come or go as she pleases; let death come today or ages hence: the steadfast do not move a step from the path of what is right.
verse.why: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On steadfastness
prasang.summary: Steadfastness: the gods kept churning the ocean past jewels and poison until they found nectar; the steady do not leave the right path whatever people say. A struck ball bounces back and a cut tree grows again.
prasang.lesson: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

verse.for_you: No honest effort on the right path is ever wasted; even a little of it protects you and carries you forward.

verse.speaker: Vasishtha
verse.setting: Vasishtha teaches the disheartened young Rama that effort, not fate, shapes his life.
verse.sanskrit: ऐहिकः प्राक्तनं हन्ति प्राक्तनोऽद्यतनं बलात् । सर्वदा पुरुषस्पन्दस्तत्रानुद्वेगवाञ्जयी ॥
verse.line: Today's effort and yesterday's keep wrestling. Whoever stays calm through it wins.
verse.translation: Present effort overcomes the past, and the past can overpower the present. It is always a contest of human striving, and the one who stays calm wins.
verse.why: Your past effort shaped today; today's effort shapes tomorrow. Don't grieve what was never in your hands.

prasang.title: Vasishtha on self-effort: fate is only your past effort
prasang.summary: Vasishtha's first teaching to Rama is a long case for self-effort. What people call fate is simply the fruit of their own past effort, and present effort can overcome it, as the stronger of two rams wins. He also says not to torment yourself over what was beyond your power, and to steer your habits gently, like raising a child.
prasang.lesson: Your past effort shaped today; today's effort shapes tomorrow. Don't grieve what was never in your hands.

verse.meaning: Vasishtha is speaking to the young prince Rama after he has lost his kingdom and is ready to give up. Vasishtha tells him that fate is not some outside force but simply the result of past effort. The present moment is a wrestling match between what was done before and what is done now. Whoever stays calm and keeps striving in this contest wins. The past can shape the present, but present effort can always overcome it. The choice is to keep moving forward or to let yesterday defeat you.
verse.for_you: You quit your job last week and the fire is bright, but the past is already pulling at you, asking if this is stubbornness. The work is yours, and that is what matters. What will test you is the quiet month when the feeling fades and only the effort remains.
verse.try_today: Notice the moment you want to quit and name it as effort, not fate.
verse.scene_line: You stand in your own kingdom, stripped of the old, and the past is already wrestling for your attention.
asks: How do I tell discipline from stubbornness?
What do I do when the feeling fades?
How do I stay calm when everything changes?

verse.speaker: Vidura
verse.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
verse.sanskrit: निश्चित्य यः प्रक्रमते नान्तर्वसति कर्मणः / अवन्ध्यकालो वश्यात्मा स वै पण्डित उच्यते
verse.line: Decide, then begin. Don't stall halfway, don't waste time, and keep yourself steady.
verse.translation: One who begins only after deciding, does not stop halfway through the work, does not waste time and keeps himself in hand, is called wise.
verse.why: Decide calmly, act steadily, forgive freely, and know what real happiness is made of.

prasang.title: Vidura Niti: the wise and the fool
prasang.summary: Sleepless before the peace talks, King Dhritarashtra calls his half-brother Vidura for counsel. Vidura describes the marks of the wise and the fool, the faults that block progress, and the six joys of life.
prasang.lesson: Decide calmly, act steadily, forgive freely, and know what real happiness is made of.

verse.for_you: You have decided to build your brand and you are in it. The work is yours and the feeling is real, but the path is still being walked. You do not need to be perfect or fast. You could keep your own hand steady on the work.
verse.try_today: Pick one small task you set aside yesterday and finish it today.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own chamber, deciding to build what is yours.
asks: What does steady look like for me today?
How do I keep my hand steady?
What is the one task I decided on?

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse.sanskrit: तं विद्याद् दुःखसंयोगवियोगं योगसंज्ञितम् । स निश्चयेन योक्तव्यो योगोऽनिर्विण्णचेतसा ॥
verse.line: Yoga is unhooking from sorrow. Practise it with resolve and a heart that doesn't lose hope.
verse.translation: Know that to be yoga: the breaking of contact with sorrow. This yoga should be practised with determination and with an undespairing mind.

words.en: separation from the union with suffering

verse.why: Moderation and gentle return, again and again, settle the mind.

prasang.title: Meditation in detail
prasang.summary: Krishna describes meditation: moderation in food and sleep, the mind like a lamp in a windless place, bringing the wandering mind back, and feeling others' joy and pain as one's own.
prasang.lesson: Moderation and gentle return, again and again, settle the mind.

story.title: Building the bridge
story.story_hook: The army stood on the shore with no boats, until a quiet monkey said he knew how to build a bridge.
story.summary: Ram waits three days for the ocean to let him pass, then loses patience. The ocean reveals that Nala can build a bridge; Nala admits his skill and the whole army hauls trees and rocks for five days until the bridge reaches Lanka.
story.lesson: Big things get built by many hands, once someone admits they know how.

anchor.speaker: Nala
anchor.setting: The army is stuck at the ocean; Nala reveals he can build a bridge, which he had not mentioned.
anchor.sanskrit: समर्थश्चाप्यहं सेतुं कर्तुं वै वरुणालये। तस्मादद्यैव बध्नन्तु सेतुं वानरपुङ्गवाः॥
anchor.line: I can build this. Let's start today.
anchor.translation: I too am able to build a bridge across the ocean. So let the best of the monkeys start building it this very day.
anchor.why: Big things get built by many hands, once someone admits they know how.
